hints: Think what happens to a single $\text{-COOH}$ group with excess $\text{SOCl}_2$, then apply it twice to $\text{HOOC-COOH}$.
walkthrough:
Recall the acyl chloride test**
You know $\text{SOCl}_2$ converts a carboxylic acid $\text{-COOH}$ into an acyl chloride $\text{-COCl}$. Here you have a dicarboxylic acid, $\text{HOOC-COOH}$, and excess reagent, so both ends react in the same way.

Draw both ends changed**
Simply replace each $\text{-OH}$ of the two $\text{-COOH}$ groups with $\text{-Cl}$. That gives $\text{Cl-C(=O)-C(=O)-Cl}$. No carbon skeleton changes, only $\text{OH}$ to $\text{Cl}$.
Final answer: $\text{ClOC-COCl}$ or $\text{Cl-C(=O)-C(=O)-Cl}$, ethanedioyl dichloride

hints: Recall the other two phosphorus chlorides that also replace $\text{-OH}$ in a carboxylic acid with $\text{-Cl}$.
walkthrough:
List the chlorinating trio**
Sit beside me and memorise this set: $\text{SOCl}_2$, $\text{PCl}_5$ and $\text{PCl}_3$ all do $\text{RCOOH}$ to $\text{RCOCl}$. Since $\text{SOCl}_2$ is already used, either of the other two is a correct different reagent.
Final answer: $\text{PCl}_3$ or $\text{PCl}_5$

hints: Think of the simplest oxidant of all, the gas in air that slowly oxidises ethanedioic acid.
Think of the classic purple oxidant used acidified that decolourises when it oxidises a reducing acid like ethanedioic acid.
walkthrough:
See ethanedioic acid as a reducing agent**
Carbon in $\text{HOOC-COOH}$ is in oxidation state +3 and can be oxidised up to +4 in $\text{CO}_2$. So you need an oxidant strong enough to take it to $2\text{CO}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$.

Name two different oxidants**
The two accepted oxidants here are oxygen, $\text{O}_2$, and acidified $\text{KMnO}_4$. The manganate(VII) reaction is the familiar titration where purple $\text{MnO}_4^-$ is reduced to colourless $\text{Mn}^{2+}$ while ethanedioate is oxidised to $\text{CO}_2$.

Final answer: 1. oxygen, $\text{O}_2$ (in air)
2. acidified potassium manganate(VII), $\text{KMnO}_4$

hints: Compare the group attached to the $\text{-COOH}$ being ionised: $\text{-COOH}$ in ethanedioic acid versus $\text{-H}$ in methanoic acid, and think about electronegativity.
Think how that neighbouring group affects the $\text{O-H}$ bond strength and the stability of the $\text{HOOCCOO}^-$ anion once $\text{H}^+$ is lost.
walkthrough:
Compare what is pulling electrons**
Write them side by side: $\text{H-COOH}$ versus $\text{HOOC-COOH}$. In methanoic acid the $\text{-COOH}$ is attached to H, but in ethanedioic acid it is attached to another $\text{C=O}$ containing $\text{COOH}$ group. Carbonyl $\text{C=O}$ is strongly electronegative and electron withdrawing by the inductive effect.

Link withdrawal to easier ionisation**
That withdrawal pulls electron density away from the $\text{O-H}$ bond being broken, weakening it so $\text{H}^+$ is released more easily. Equally important, the negative charge on the $\text{HOOCCOO}^-$ anion is dispersed and stabilised by the adjacent electron withdrawing $\text{C=O}$. A more stable conjugate base means a stronger acid.

Final answer: The second $\text{C=O}$ / $\text{COOH}$ group is electron withdrawing.
This weakens the $\text{O-H}$ bond and stabilises the $\text{HOOCCOO}^-$ anion, favouring dissociation, so ethanedioic acid is stronger.

hints: Work backwards from benzene-1,4-dicarboxylic acid: step 2 must oxidise alkyl side chains to $\text{-COOH}$, so what dialkylbenzene gives para diacid?
walkthrough:
Reverse the oxidation**
Step 2 converts J into $\text{HOOC-C}_6\text{H}_4\text{-COOH}$ with 1,4 positions. Strong oxidation of an alkylbenzene gives benzoic acid, with the alkyl carbon becoming the $\text{-COOH}$ carbon. So to get two $\text{-COOH}$ groups para to each other, J must have two alkyl groups para to each other.

Choose the simplest alkyl**
The simplest route is two methyl groups, so J is 1,4-dimethylbenzene, para-xylene. Draw a benzene ring with $\text{CH}_3$ at opposite corners.
Final answer: 1,4-dimethylbenzene: $\text{CH}_3\text{-C}_6\text{H}_4\text{-CH}_3$ with methyl groups para to each other

hints: For benzene to 1,4-dimethylbenzene, recall the electrophilic substitution using a chloroalkane with a halogen carrier catalyst.
For methyl groups to carboxylic acid groups, recall the vigorous hot oxidant that oxidises the whole side chain, with alkali then acidification.
walkthrough:
Make the C-C bond to the ring**
Step 1 is Friedel-Crafts alkylation. Use chloromethane, $\text{CH}_3\text{Cl}$, with catalyst $\text{AlCl}_3$ to generate the $\text{CH}_3^+$ electrophile. This puts methyl groups on the ring to give J.

Oxidise side chains fully**
Step 2 is side chain oxidation. Heat with alkaline $\text{KMnO}_4$ which oxidises each $\text{-CH}_3$ right up to $\text{-COO}^-$, then acidify to get $\text{-COOH}$. Conditions must be hot and alkaline, followed by dilute acid.

Final answer: step 1: $\text{CH}_3\text{Cl}$ + $\text{AlCl}_3$ (Friedel-Crafts alkylation)
step 2: hot alkaline $\text{KMnO}_4$, then dilute acid

hints: Recall that diacid plus diol gives ester links with loss of water, so join $\text{-C(=O)-OH + HO-CH}_2\text{-}$ to $\text{-C(=O)-O-CH}_2\text{-}$.
Build one repeat unit containing the para $\text{-C}_6\text{H}_4\text{-}$ from the diacid and the $\text{-CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{-}$ from the diol, showing the $\text{-C(=O)-O-}$ fully displayed.
walkthrough:
Spot the polyester reaction**
Carboxylic acid plus alcohol gives ester plus water. Here a diacid plus a diol gives a polyester. Each $\text{-COOH + HO-}$ pair becomes $\text{-C(=O)-O- + H}_2\text{O}$.

Assemble exactly one repeat unit**
Take the diacid residue $\text{-C(=O)-C}_6\text{H}_4\text{-C(=O)-}$ keeping the 1,4 para substitution, and join it to the diol residue $\text{-O-CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{-O-}$. Show both $\text{C=O}$ and $\text{C-O}$ bonds fully displayed: $\text{-C(=O)-C}_6\text{H}_4\text{-C(=O)-O-C}_2\text{H}_4\text{-O-}$. That is one complete repeat unit.
Final answer: One repeat unit: $\text{-C(=O)-C}_6\text{H}_4\text{-C(=O)-O-CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{-O-}$ with para benzene and fully displayed $\text{-C(=O)-O-}$ ester groups

hints: Think what small molecule is lost when $\text{-COOH}$ and $\text{-OH}$ join, and what that tells you about the polymerisation type and linkage name.
walkthrough:
Name type and link together**
Because water is eliminated at each join, this is condensation polymerisation, not addition. The $\text{-C(=O)-O-}$ link formed between acid and alcohol is always called an ester link, so this polymer is a polyester.

Final answer: type of polymerisation: condensation
linkage: ester
